title: Follow the Grail
subtitle: Malory, Books XIII–XVII, in seventeen stops
blurb: The whole quest, read in order, with a line of commentary at each stop telling you what to watch for. About four hours' reading; you can stop and resume anywhere.
intro: Malory's Grail quest is a translation of the French *Queste del Saint Graal*, and it follows its source closely — which means it inherits the *Queste*'s verdict that the Round Table is not good enough. What Malory adds is grief. Read it watching for two things: how systematically the fellowship is measured and found wanting, and how often Malory pauses to note the cost of the measuring.

stops.note: Letters appear on the empty seat, and a sword arrives in a floating stone. Watch Lancelot refuse to try — he already knows why he would fail.
Galahad takes the Siege Perilous and nothing happens to him. From this moment every knight in the hall is measurably not him.

The vessel enters, covered in white samite. The knights vow the quest — and in the same chapter Arthur tells Gawain the vow has nearly killed him. Read to the end of the chapter; the whole argument of this portal is in those four paragraphs.
The departure, and the grief of the court. Arthur says he will never see them all together again, and he is right.
Galahad's white shield with the red cross, made by Joseph of Arimathea's blood. The Grail's Christian genealogy, made visible as a heraldic device.
Gawain is told plainly that he will find nothing, because he has not confessed in years. The English tradition's favourite knight, dismissed in a paragraph.
Lancelot, half asleep at a ruined chapel, watches the Grail heal a sick man in front of him and cannot move.
The voice: harder than stone, more bitter than wood, more naked and barren than the fig tree. He is told to withdraw.
The confession. Twenty-four years, and the first time in his life he asks God for anything. The best writing in the quest.
Merlin likens the Round Table to the world. The quest's own account of what the fellowship was for.
Percival, tempted by a lady on a ship, wounds himself through the thigh as penance. The Queste's ethic at its most extreme.
Bors's choice: his own brother being flogged, or a stranger about to be raped, and only time to reach one. He chooses the stranger. The best moral problem in the book.
Lionel comes for him, and Bors will not raise a sword against his brother. The choice is not made costless.
The ship, the bed, and the sword of the strange girdles. Malory's most openly allegorical stretch.
Percival's sister gives a dish of blood to cure a stranger, and dies of it. She achieves as much as Galahad and the text never gives her a name.
The Mass at Corbenic, and the figure that comes out of the vessel. Galahad sees what tongue cannot tell, and asks to die.
Sarras. The Grail is taken up to heaven and never seen again; two of the three are dead; Bors rides home alone to a court he knows is finished.

after: Now read Book XVIII, chapter i. Malory's first sentence about what happened next is one of the quietest and worst in the book.
